function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **zelarhq/nodejs-welcome** repository.  
It contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node JS image |
| `k8s.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main` |

> **NOTE** – The repo is a Node.js project, so the Dockerfile uses a Node base image (the helper function you saw only supports Python images).  
> The GitHub Actions workflow pushes the image to **GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io)** – you can change it to Docker Hub or another registry if you prefer.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Build a minimal Node.js image for the app
# ------------------------------------
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why node:18‑alpine?*  
> Alpine gives you a small image (~70 MB) and Node 18 is the LTS version that most projects still use.  
> If your `package.json` requires a different Node version, change the `FROM` line accordingly.

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAML (`k8s.yaml`)

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
# ------------------------------------
# Deployment + Service for nodejs-welcome
# ------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

### What this does

| Section | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `Deployment` | Runs 2 replicas of the container, automatically rolling‑updating when the image changes |
| `Service` | Exposes the pods on port 80 inside the cluster (you can change `type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access) |

> **Tip** – If you’re deploying to a cloud provider that supports `LoadBalancer`, change `type: ClusterIP` to `type: LoadBalancer` and the provider will provision an external IP for you.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
# ------------------------------------
# CI pipeline that builds & pushes the Docker image
# ------------------------------------
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑arch support)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Login to ghcr.io
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the image and push it
      - name: Build & push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

      # Optional: Run tests (if you have a test script)
      # - name: Run tests
      #   run: npm test
```

### How it works

1. **Trigger** – Runs on every push to `main`.  
2. **Checkout** – Pulls the repo into the runner.  
3. **Buildx** – Enables multi‑arch builds (useful if you later want ARM images).  
4. **Login** – Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to `ghcr.io`.  
5. **Build & Push** – Builds the image from the Dockerfile and pushes it to `ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>:latest`.  

> **If you want to push to Docker Hub** replace the login step with:
> ```yaml
> - name: Login to Docker Hub
>   uses: docker/login-action@v3
>   with:
>     username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
>     password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}
> ```
> and change the `tags:` line to `docker.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest`.

---

## 4. Adding, Committing & Pushing

Once you’ve added the three files above to the repo, run the following commands locally:

```bash
# 1. Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# 2. Commit with a meaningful message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 3. Push to the remote
git push origin main
```

> If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.  
> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run and build the image.

---

## 5. Quick sanity check

1. **Build locally** (optional but recommended):

   ```bash
   docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .
   docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:local
   ```

   Visit `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is running.

2. **Deploy to a cluster** (e.g., Minikube or a cloud cluster):

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
   ```

   Verify pods are running:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pods
   ```

   And expose the service (if you used `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`).

---

### Recap

- **Dockerfile** – Builds a lightweight Node.js image.  
- **k8s.yaml** – Deployment + Service for Kubernetes.  
- **ci.yml** – GitHub Actions that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main`.  
- **Git commands** – Add, commit, push.

Drop these files into the repo, push, and you’ll have a fully automated build pipeline and ready‑to‑deploy Kubernetes manifests! 🚀
